title: Joel
subtitle: locusts, a fast, the Spirit poured out, and the day of the LORD
lead: Joel is a short book that starts with an insect plague and ends with the judgment of the nations. A swarm of locusts, four waves of them, has eaten the harvest, and drought and fire have finished what the swarm left. The offerings have stopped in the Temple because there is no grain or wine to give. Joel calls the whole community to mourn, to fast and to gather at the house of the LORD. Then the day of the LORD comes into view: an army like the locusts, with the LORD himself at its head.

At the center of the book is one sentence: "Even now, the LORD declares, turn back to me with your whole heart." Joel quotes the oldest creed of Israel, that the LORD is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and great in loyal love, and adds that he changes his mind about the harm. The LORD answers with grain, wine and oil, and gives back the years the locusts ate. Then the book looks ahead: the Spirit poured out on all flesh, the sun turned dark and the moon to blood, rescue for everyone who calls on the LORD's name, and the nations tried in the Valley of Jehoshaphat. Peter used these words at Pentecost.

Joel gives no king and no date, and his book has been placed in almost every century from the ninth to the fourth BC. What is certain is that the prophets who came after him in the Twelve, and the New Testament writers, read him closely, and that he read the prophets before him closely too.
facts: Hebrew Yo'el, "the LORD is God"; Greek Ioel; Latin Ioel
Joel son of Pethuel (Greek "Bethuel"). Nothing else is known of him

Debated. A ninth-century setting in the reign of the boy-king Joash (Stuart); a late-pre-exilic date (older Jewish tradition places him under Manasseh); or the Persian period, about 500 to 350 BC, the commonest view in critical scholarship (Wolff, Crenshaw, Barton)
Judah and Jerusalem. The Temple stands, with priests and elders; no king is named; a locust plague and drought have stopped the offerings

Prophetic poetry: a call to lament, a summons to fast, a salvation oracle, a promise of the Spirit and a vision of the judgment of the nations. Often called a bridge between classical prophecy and apocalyptic

The Hebrew Bible has 4 chapters (20, 27, 5 and 21 verses). English 2:28-32 is Hebrew 3:1-5, and English chapter 3 is Hebrew chapter 4. The Greek editions differ: Rahlfs's Septuagint and the Greek Orthodox lectionary number as the Hebrew does (their 3:1-5 and 4:1-21), while Swete's edition, the Latin Vulgate and the English Bibles number as the English do. This Plain and all its references use the English numbers; notes that cite the Greek give the other numbering as well
The second of the Twelve (the Minor Prophets) in the Hebrew order: Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah. In the Greek order it is fourth: Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah

The Leningrad Codex, the Septuagint as printed by Swete (Codex Vaticanus), and the Dead Sea Scroll transcriptions of 4Q78 (4QXII-c), 4Q82 (4QXII-g) and Mur88 (the Wadi Murabba'at scroll of the Twelve)
authorship: The book opens with a title: "The LORD's word came to Joel, son of Pethuel." Joel is a common name, "the LORD is God", and his father's name is found nowhere else. The book says nothing of his tribe, town or work. It shows a man at home in the Temple and in the older prophets, who speaks with the priests and the elders as his audience. The Lives of the Prophets, an early Jewish-Christian collection of uncertain date, makes him a man of the tribe of Reuben; this is legend.

Held by Stuart and others. The book's place between Hosea and Amos in the Hebrew order of the Twelve, which seems chronological; the lack of any mention of Assyria or Babylon; the enemies named (Tyre, Sidon, Philistia, Egypt and Edom) as the neighbors of the ninth century (2 Kings 8:20-22; 2 Chronicles 21:16-17); and the leadership of priests and elders, which fits the regency of the priest Jehoiada for the boy Joash (2 Kings 11-12).

The commonest view in critical scholarship (Wolff, Crenshaw, Barton). The Temple is working and the priests lead the nation, with no king; the exile and scattering of Judah are in the past (3:2); Greeks are the buyers of slaves (3:6); Jerusalem has walls (2:7, 9); and the book uses Isaiah 13, Ezekiel 30, Obadiah 15-17, Amos 1:2 and 9:13, Micah 4:3, Exodus 34:6 and Jonah 4:2, which suggests that it comes after them. The vocabulary and the mixed prophecy and apocalypse of chapters 2-3 are said to fit this age as well.

Bernhard Duhm (1911) separated the locust poem of chapters 1-2 from the apocalyptic chapters 3-4 (Hebrew numbering) and ascribed them to different writers. Most scholars now defend the unity of the book, seeing a single author, or a single editor, whose book moves from a past disaster to a future judgment. The book's use of the same phrases across its parts (the day of the LORD, 'dry' and 'ashamed', 'Zion') supports unity.

Siegfried Bergler (1988) called Joel a 'scriptural interpreter': a writer who works from earlier prophetic texts. John Barton and others stress how many lines of Joel are found elsewhere (Joel 1:15 = Isaiah 13:6; 2:13 = Jonah 4:2; 3:10 reverses Isaiah 2:4; 3:16 = Amos 1:2; 3:18 shares a clause with Amos 9:13). Which book gave and which received is often unclear, and the answer depends on the date.

audience.to: The people of Judah and Jerusalem, gathered around the Temple: the elders, the priests and 'everyone who lives in the land', in a year of locusts, drought and fire. The nation is led by elders and priests, and no king is named. The book speaks directly to the priests and farmers, to the drunkards who have lost their wine, and in the end to 'the children of Zion'.
audience.why: To turn a disaster into repentance and hope. The plague has stopped the offerings, so the loss is both a famine and a crisis of worship. Joel tells his hearers that the plague is a sign of the day of the LORD, calls them to a fast and a sacred assembly, gives the priests the words to pray, and relays the LORD's answer: the land restored, the shame ended, the Spirit given to all. He then widens the picture to the day when the nations that wronged Judah will be judged. Knowing this audience, we read the terror of chapters 1-2 as an invitation to turn, not only as a threat, and the promise of chapter 2 as an answer to the priests' prayer of 2:17, if 2:18 reports what happened (the note on 2:18 keeps the other reading open).
views: The audience is the Judah of the ninth or eighth century, where the priests and elders lead because the king is a child or is not the point. The enemies are Tyre, Sidon, Philistia, Egypt and Edom; the Greeks are traders on the coast.

The audience is the restored community of the fifth or fourth century, governed by priests and elders without a king, who have known the exile, and for whom the scattering of 3:2 is memory. The prophet draws on Scripture that the community already knows.
Some scholars (Ahlström) think the book was shaped for use in the Temple on days of fasting and prayer, which would make 'audience' every community that used it.

outline: Title: the LORD's word to Joel
Hear this: a plague without equal, and four locusts that ate everything
The drunkards, the farmers and the vinedressers are called to mourn; the land mourns
The priests are called to sackcloth, a fast and a sacred assembly
Alas for the day! The day of the LORD is close; Joel's prayer, and the animals
The horn in Zion; the army like locusts that the LORD leads
"Even now": turn back; the creed; "Who knows?"
The fast and assembly; the priests' prayer between the porch and the altar
The LORD's answer: the northern one driven away, the rains, the lost years given back
The Spirit poured out on all flesh; signs in the sky; everyone who calls on the LORD is rescued
The nations judged in the Valley of Jehoshaphat; Tyre, Sidon and Philistia
The summons to war; the harvest and the winepress; the LORD roars from Zion
Zion blessed: wine, milk, water and a spring; Egypt and Edom waste; the LORD lives in Zion

lenses.name: History and fulfillment
lenses.desc: A locust plague, drought and fire in Judah, and the nation's fast at the Temple. The date is debated: the ninth or eighth century (the days of Joash or after) or the Babylonian fall and Persian times (the sixth to the fourth centuries). The evidence for each: no king, a working Temple, priests and elders, Tyre and Sidon, Greeks as slave buyers, the exile in the past, borrowing from other prophets.

lenses.name: Critical scholarship
lenses.desc: The unity of chapters 1-2 and 3; the locust poem and the army poem (2:1-11); the 'northern one' (2:20); Joel's dense quotation of and by other prophets (Exodus 10, Isaiah 13, Ezekiel 30, Obadiah 15, 17, Amos 1:2 and 9:13, Micah 4:3); the Hebrew text and the Septuagint; the Dead Sea Scrolls; Joel's place in the Twelve.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak on the locusts (1:4), the northern one (2:20), the teacher or the rain (2:23) and the valley (3:2), as the notes at those verses report them; the Talmud (Sukkah 52a) on the northern one and Numbers Rabbah 15:25 on prophecy for all Israel in the age to come; the fast of 2:12-17 and the Mishnah's fast days; Joel 2:13 in the liturgy; the valley of Jehoshaphat and the judgment of the nations. Not checked for this edition, and so not credited with any view: the Targum of Joel and the other medieval commentaries.

lenses.name: Christian reading
lenses.desc: Acts 2 and Romans 10:13; Revelation 6:12, 9:7-11 and 14:14-20; Jerome on the four locusts and on 2:23; the Ash Wednesday reading of 2:12-18; Pentecostal and charismatic use of 2:28; Calvin on Acts 2. Not checked for this edition, and so not credited with any view: Ephrem, Cyril of Alexandria, Theodoret, Chrysostom, Luther and Calvin on Joel itself, and Pusey.

lenses.name: Still to come
lenses.desc: The day of the LORD as a future day (2:30-32; 3:1-17); the valley of decision; the final war and restoration, as dispensational, amillennial and Jewish messianic readers see them.

sections.b:
Joel is easiest to read as a sequence of acts. In act one (1:2-20) the prophet describes a disaster and calls one group after another to mourn. In act two (2:1-17) the horn sounds, the day of the LORD arrives as an army, and the LORD himself calls the nation to turn back; the priests are given a prayer. In act three (2:18-27) the LORD answers: the enemy is driven off and the harvest returns. In act four (2:28-3:21) the promise widens to the Spirit on all flesh, the judgment of the nations, and the blessing of Zion.

Notice what Joel does not say. He does not name a sin that caused the plague, as Amos 4:9 does. He does not say that the fast will force the LORD's hand: "Who knows?" He does not describe the Spirit's coming as a replacement for the Temple. The book assumes the Temple and its offerings from first to last, and ends with the LORD living in Zion.

Joel 1:4 and 2:25 use four Hebrew words, gazam, 'arbeh, yeleq and chasil, that English Bibles translate in many ways ("locust", "grasshopper", "palmerworm", "cankerworm"). No one knows exactly what each insect was. The Plain gives four distinct English words (the cutting, swarming, hopping and stripping locust). The four have been read as four stages of the locust's growth, four kinds of locust, four poetic names, or four empires. The note at 1:4 gives the views. Locust plagues are real: a swarm in Palestine and Syria in 1915 stripped the country, and observers use the same words Joel does.

sections.h: Real locusts, an army, or the end of the world?
sections.b: Chapter 2 pictures the same invader as an army that climbs walls and enters windows like a thief. Is it locusts, a human army from the north, or a heavenly host? The book itself mixes the images: the army looks like horses (2:4, as locusts do), it is led by the LORD (2:11) and is "my great army" (2:25), and it is dealt with as "the northern one" (2:20). The three readings are old. Locusts: a real plague told with military language. A human army: an invasion told with locust images, as Assyria is a razor and a flood in Isaiah. An end-time power: the enemy of the last days, as Gog in Ezekiel 38-39. The Plain keeps the wording and the doubt.

Joel is full of lines found elsewhere. Joel 1:15 is word for word Isaiah 13:6 ("It comes like havoc from the Almighty"). Joel 2:2 ("never before, never again") is from the plague story in Exodus 10:14. Joel 2:13 is Exodus 34:6 in Nehemiah's and Jonah's form. Joel 2:28 is close to Ezekiel 39:29 and Isaiah 44:3. Joel 3:10 reverses Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3. Joel 3:16 is Amos 1:2, and Joel 3:18 is close to Amos 9:13. Joel 2:32 and 3:17 are close to Obadiah 17. Whether Joel borrowed or was borrowed from is the main reason the date is argued. The Plain gives the same English for the same Hebrew whenever the earlier book is already on the site.

The Hebrew Bible counts Hosea to Malachi as one scroll, "the Twelve", and Sirach 49:10 praises "the twelve prophets". Joel is second in the Hebrew order (Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah), and fourth in the Greek order (Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah). Catchwords join it to its neighbors: wine, grain and oil in Hosea 14 and Joel 1; Joel 3:16 and 3:18 with Amos 1:2 and 9:13; the day of the LORD and Zion's survivors with Obadiah 15-17; the creed of 2:13 with Jonah 4:2. Some scholars (Nogalski, Schart, Sweeney) argue that the Twelve were put together as a single book with Joel as a bridge; others (Ben Zvi, Barton) doubt that the Twelve were meant to be read as one. The Plain takes no side.

The Hebrew text of Joel is in good condition. The Greek (Septuagint) of Joel is a close translation, with the differences noted in the variants: "from my Spirit" (2:28), "heifers" for the seeds (1:17), "the food for righteousness" for "the early rain" (2:23), "those who bring good news" for "survivors" (2:32), "Galilee of the foreigners" (3:4), a gentle man as a fighter (3:11), and a different verb in 3:21. Numbering. Rahlfs's Greek and the Greek Orthodox lectionary number Joel as the Hebrew does (3:1-5 for what English calls 2:28-32, and 4:1-21); Swete's edition, the Vulgate and English Bibles use three chapters. This Plain uses the English numbers; the notes give the Greek numbers where they differ. Three Dead Sea scrolls preserve parts of Joel in the transcription read for this Plain: 4Q78 (4QXII-c), with parts of 1:10 to 2:23 and 3:6-21; 4Q82 (4QXII-g), with parts of 1:12-14, 2:2-13 and 3:4-20; and Mur88, a scroll of the Twelve from the Wadi Murabba'at, with parts of 2:20 and 2:26 to 3:16. Where the printout shows them they agree with the Masoretic Text apart from small spellings and the places listed in the variants (1:12, 1:17, 2:19, 3:1, 3:3 and 3:21 among them). Other places where a scroll differs in small ways are noted in the notes at 2:11 and 3:19. At 3:8 the scroll 4Q78 shows "of Armies" only as a restoration, which is not a reading. The Vulgate (Jerome) is cited as a later witness for reception; the Aramaic Targum of the Prophets and the Syriac Peshitta were not read for this edition.

Jews read Joel 2:13 in the Mishnah's order of fasts for rain (Taanit 2:1) and the 'thirteen attributes' of the LORD from which it comes (Exodus 34:6-7) are central in penitential prayer. Christians read Joel 2:12-18 on Ash Wednesday, in the Catholic and in the common lectionaries, and Joel 2:28-32 in Peter's sermon at Pentecost; the Greek Orthodox lectionary reads Joel 2:23-3:5 (its numbering, English 2:23-32) among the readings of Pentecost Vespers. In the Pentecostal and charismatic churches Joel 2:23 and 2:28-29 are often applied to a revival of the Spirit in the last days.

spec.title: Where is their God? The book's answer in three steps
spec.body: My own reading, which overlaps with commentary on 2:17-27 but arranges it as a staircase. The priests' prayer asks the question of the nations: 'Where is their God?' (2:17). The book answers it three times, each nearer than the last. The LORD is 'among Israel' (2:27, in the midst). He pours his Spirit 'on all flesh' (2:28, on the people). He 'lives in Zion' (3:17, 21, in the city). The movement is from presence among a people, to presence in every person, to presence in a place. Commentators discuss each verse; I do not know a published argument that sets the three together as one answer.

prompts: A drawing sketched onto a scroll in ink, ochre and charcoal: a swarm of locusts crossing a hillside field in four distinct bands, each band a different size and color, from large to small, in the style of an ancient manuscript mixed with cave drawing and modern line art, soft hand-drawn edges, no hard rectangle.

Priests lying in rough goat-hair sackcloth on the stone floor between a temple porch and an altar, at night, an oil lamp beside them, drawn in brown ink with washes of red ochre as if on old parchment, soft torn edges.
The spring from the house of the LORD

A thin stream of water running from beneath the doorway of a small temple down a dry valley of acacia trees, turning the ground green as it goes, sketched in blue and green washes on a tan scroll, loose hand-drawn lines, soft edges.

A wide valley filled with crowds of small figures, above them a sun and a moon darkened to circles, in the middle a great sickle and a winepress, drawn in the style of an ancient manuscript with modern line art, ink and ochre on a scroll, soft edges.
reading: A full commentary on the Hebrew, with a thorough treatment of the date and the quotations.
Hans Walter Wolff, Joel and Amos (Hermeneia)
The classic critical commentary; argues for a date near 400 BC and for the book's unity.
John Barton, Joel and Obadiah (Old Testament Library)
A clear commentary that reads the book as a unified prophetic work and stresses its use of earlier texts.
Duane Garrett, Hosea, Joel (New American Commentary)
An evangelical commentary on the Hebrew with a full discussion of the date.
Ronald Simkins, Yahweh's Activity in History and Nature in the Book of Joel
A study of the relation between the locust plague and the day of the LORD.
James Nogalski, Literary Precursors to the Book of the Twelve
The case that Joel is a bridge in the Twelve.
